(For the purpose of convenience, the parties are hereafter referred to as per their rank before the Tribunal).
2.

The petitioner filed the above O.P. under Sections 140 and 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988,
claiming compensation for the injuries sustained in a motor vehicle accident that occurred on 04.12.2010.

According to the petitioner, on 04.12.2010 at about 7.30 a.m., while he was standing by the side of the road, a Maruti car bearing Reg.No.KL-11K-2203 driven by the 2nd respondent in a rash and negligent manner hit him down and as a result of the accident, the petitioner sustained serious injuries.
3. The 1st respondent is the owner, the 2nd respondent is the driver and 3rd respondent is the insurer of the offending vehicle.
According to the petitioner, the accident occurred due to the negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle.

The quantum of compensation claimed in the O.P.
is Rs.2,20,000/-.
4. The insurance company filed a written statement, admitting the 2025:KER:33015 accident as well as policy, but disputing the negligence on the part of the driver of the offending vehicle.
5. The evidence in the case consists of the documentary evidence Exts.A1 to A7 and C1.
No evidence was adduced by the respondents.

6. After evaluating the evidence on record, the Tribunal found negligence on the part of the driver of the offending vehicle, awarded a total compensation of Rs. 3,97,900/- (rounded to 3,98,000/-) and directed the insurer to pay the same.
7. Aggrieved by the quantum of compensation awarded by the Tribunal, the petitioner preferred this appeal.
8. Now the point that arises for consideration is the following:

Whether the quantum of compensation awarded by the Tribunal is just and Ravindran vs C.P.Rajan on 10 April, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/134594648/
2 reasonable?
9.

Heard Sri.Zubair Pulikool, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner/appellant, and Sri.
Mathews Jaocb, the learned Senior Standing Counsel as instructed by Sri.P. Jacob Mathew, the learned Standing Counsel for the 3rd respondent.
10. The Point: In this case the accident as well as valid insurance policy of the offending vehicle are admitted.
One of the contentions raised by 2025:KER:33015 the learned counsel for the petitioner is regarding the income of the petitioner as fixed by the Tribunal.
According to him, the petitioner was working as Security guard, earning Rs.10,000/- per month, but the Tribunal fixed his monthly income at Rs.5,000/-.
The learned counsel for the insurer would argue that the income fixed by the tribunal is reasonable.
11. Ext.A3 is the identity card and A6 is the cash voucher issued by P.S Security Agency.
In Ext.A6 it is stated that, the petitioner was earning Rs.700/- per day.
According to the learned counsel, he used to work for a period of 15 days in a month.
The petitioner has not adduced any evidence to prove Exts.A3 and A6.
Even then, from Exts.A3 and A6 it can be safely concluded that the petitioner was working as Security in the above company.
As per the dictum laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the decision in Ramachandrappa v. Manager, Royal Sundaram Alliance Insurance Co. Ltd.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: , the notional income of a coolie, in the year 2010 will come to Rs.7500/-.
Therefore, considering the fact that the petitioner was working as Security in a company, his notional income is fixed at Rs. 8,500/-, for the purpose of computing the loss of disability.

12. In the accident the petitioner sustained the following injuries:
1. Fracture left femur middle x 1/3 comminuted 2025:KER:33015 2.
fracture
left fibula

3. Swelling, deformity, tenderness, abnormal mobility and crepitation present over middle 3rd thigh.
4. Swelling, tenderness present over the lateral malleolus 13.
As per Exhibit C1 disability certificate the petitioner suffered 33% permanent physical disability.
It was issued by the medical board.
The Tribunal, has accepted the permanent physical disability of the petitioner as such and hence, I do not find any grounds to disbelieve the same.
Therefore, the permanent physical disability of the petitioner is accepted as 33%, as fixed by the Tribunal.
14. On the date of accident, the petitioner was aged 50 years.

Therefore, 10% of the monthly income is to be added towards future prospects, as held in the decision in National Insurance Co. Ltd v.
Pranay Sethi [(2017) 16 SCC 680] and the multiplier to be applied is 13, as held in Sarla Verma v.
Delhi Transport Corporation, [(2009) 6 SCC 121].

3 15.
Towards loss of earning, the tribunal has awarded only Rs.30,000/- being the income for 6 months @ Rs.5,000/-.
Considering the nature of the injuries sustained and the percentage of disability suffered by the petitioner, the petitioner might have lost income at least for a period of 9 2025:KER:33015 months.

Therefore, towards 'loss of income' the petitioner is entitled to get a sum of Rs. 76,500/- (8500 x 9 months).
16.
The Tribunal has not awarded any amount on the heads 'pain and sufferings', 'loss of amenities of life' and 'extra nourishment'.
17. The petitioner sustained serious injuries in the accident and was treated as inpatient for 12 days.

Because of the injuries sustained, the percentage of disability suffered and the length of treatment undergone by the petitioner, I hold that, the petitioner is entitled to get compensation on the heads 'pain and sufferings', 'loss of amenities of life' and 'extra nourishment' a sum of Rs.75,000/-,
75,000/- and 8,000/- respectively.
18.
No change is required, in the amounts awarded on other heads, as the compensation awarded on those heads appears to be just and reasonable.
